Lane by Lane

A lane for every road user in Cyberabad, wherever the road is wide enough, watched by cameras that understand lanes.

  • Vision monitoring
  • Lane discipline

01 · THE PROBLEM

One road, everyone fighting for the same space

On most Cyberabad roads a cyclist, a scooter, a car and a city bus share one strip of asphalt. Two-wheelers weave between cars, cars squeeze cyclists to the kerb, and buses sit behind all of them. The 23 km solar-roofed cycle track along the Outer Ring Road, 4.5 m wide and open since October 2023, shows that separation works. This proposal takes it into the city with one rule: the width of the road decides what it can offer.

What the data says

26%of daily trips are on two-wheelers, against 7% by car. The biggest group of motorists has no lane of its own.
42%of trips are on foot or by cycle. That is about 7 million trips a day on streets with little space for them.
20.3 km/haverage road speed at 7 PM. A 10 km trip takes 29.5 minutes, against 18.1 minutes at 2 AM.
3,385more buses needed. The city runs 3,418, about half of what its population calls for.
803fatal road accidents in the Cyberabad police area in 2025. Two-wheeler riders were 52.8% of the dead and pedestrians 33.5%.
10,640 tof CO2 from transport every day, from 4.8 million vehicles.

Sources: SHIFT Transport, Transport Analytics Hub for trips, speeds, buses and emissions, which cover the Hyderabad metropolitan area. Telangana Today, 23 December 2025 for Cyberabad accident data.

02 · THE COST OF BAD DRIVING

Careless driving is paid for in lives, time and fuel

Congestion is not only too many vehicles. A large part of it is how they are driven. One vehicle in the wrong lane forces everyone behind it to brake, swerve or squeeze past, and each of those moves has a cost.

Lives803 fatal road accidents in the Cyberabad police area in 2025. More than half the dead were on two-wheelers.
TimeAt the evening peak, every kilometre takes over a minute longer than it does on a clear road.
FuelEach sudden brake throws away fuel that was just burned to get up to speed. Stop-and-go traffic repeats that hundreds of times a trip.
AirFuel burned while crawling and idling becomes exhaust at street level, where people walk, cycle and wait for buses.

On the Outer Ring Road: slow vehicles in the fast lanes

The ORR already has lane rules. Since July 2023, lanes 1 and 2 next to the median are for 80 to 120 km/h, and lanes 3 and 4 are for 40 to 80 km/h and heavy vehicles. The rules are widely ignored. A slow vehicle in lane 1 makes fast traffic brake late and pass on the left, and two slow trucks side by side close half the carriageway. Try each case.

A simplified model with trucks at 45 to 50 km/h and cars at 55 to 100 km/h. Long orange shapes are trucks, and the number on each vehicle is its speed. A vehicle has to slow down before it changes lanes, and a red mark shows it braking. It shows the pattern, not measured traffic.

  • Enforce the lane rules that exist. Cameras flag any vehicle below 80 km/h that holds lane 1 or 2, and any heavy vehicle outside lanes 3 and 4.
  • Say it on the road. Overhead boards and lane markings repeat one instruction: keep left unless overtaking.
  • Tell the fleet, not only the driver. Violations by commercial vehicles also go to the owner who sets the schedule.
  • Lay-bys and rest areas keep tired drivers and parked trucks off the carriageway.

03 · DEDICATED LANES

What can your road fit?

Drag the slider to the width of a road you know, measured wall to wall (the right of way). The picture shows the road as it typically is today on the left and as proposed on the right.

30 m wide

TodayProposed

Space, kerb to centreEach side

On this road

    The "today" half is a typical picture of a road of this width with mixed traffic. It is not a survey of any one road.

    Widths are indicative. The Indian Roads Congress code for urban roads (IRC:86-2018) sets 3.5 m as the standard lane and 1.8 m as the minimum clear walking width. On tighter roads this proposal narrows general lanes to as little as 3.0 m to make room for the other lanes, which a road engineer must approve for each stretch.

    At the junction

    Lanes are easy between junctions and hard at them. This is how one approach on a full corridor works. Traffic moves from left to right.

    1. Boarding island. The bus stops in its own lane. Passengers wait on an island between the bus lane and the cycle track.
    2. Raised crossing. The cycle track rises to footpath level at the stop, so cyclists slow down and passengers cross on the level.
    3. Merge zone. Before the junction, vehicles turning left may cross into the bus lane here and nowhere else.
    4. Two-wheeler waiting box. Scooters and motorbikes wait ahead of the cars and clear the junction first.
    5. Crossing with a refuge. Pedestrians cross one carriageway at a time, with a safe place to wait at the median.
    6. Junction camera. One camera watches the bus lane, the merge zone and the waiting box.

    Room for everyone

    Wheelchairs and prams

    A ramp at every crossing, tactile paving, and a footpath kept clear to at least 1.8 m.

    Women and night travel

    Lighting on footpaths, cycle tracks and bus stops, and stops that can be seen from the road.

    Children and older people

    30 km/h colony streets, refuges at medians, and signal times set for slower walkers.

    Autos, cabs and delivery riders

    Marked pick-up and loading bays on every block, so nobody has to stop in a lane.

    Street vendors

    Vending spaces in the kerb zone, off the footpath and off the cycle track.

    04 · THE VISION SYSTEM

    Cameras that understand lanes

    Paint alone gets ignored. Cameras at junctions and between them watch the lanes, and vision software works out what each vehicle is, which lane it is in and which way it is going.

    1. SeeCameras at junctions and mid-block watch every lane.
    2. UnderstandSoftware identifies the vehicle type, its lane and its direction.
    3. FlagA vehicle in the wrong lane is flagged, with its number plate from the same clip.
    4. ReviewA traffic police officer confirms the clip before anything is issued.
    5. ActA warning first, an e-challan on repeats, and a public score for every corridor.

    What it detects

    It builds on what the city already runs

    25.93 lakhe-challans issued by Cyberabad police in 2025. The back end for notices exists. Source
    14ORR locations where the ORR authority has proposed AI cameras for wrong-way driving, slow movement and lane discipline. Source
    NextLane by Lane takes the same idea off the expressway and onto city streets, where the lanes are being drawn.
    • A person decides. No notice goes out until an officer has confirmed the clip.
    • Warnings first. For the first 30 days on a new corridor, a violation brings a warning, not a fine.
    • Privacy by default. Only clips of flagged violations are kept, and no faces are stored.
    • Open data. Anonymous counts by lane and hour are published for anyone to check.
    05 · LANE DISCIPLINE

    Make staying in lane the normal thing to do

    Enforcement catches the few. Habit changes the many.

    1. Colour codeThe same colours on every road: green for cycles, blue for two-wheelers, orange for buses.
    2. Learn firstFor the first 30 days on a new corridor, a violation brings a warning SMS. Fines begin after that.
    3. Corridor scoresWeekly lane compliance goes on roadside boards. Resident associations and tech parks on the best corridor are recognised each quarter.
    4. Fleets pledgeDelivery, bike-taxi and cab operators share compliance scores with their riders and reward clean records.
    5. Keep leftOne instruction for the ORR and every divided road, on overhead boards, toll receipts and navigation alerts.

The emission rates per kilometre are assumptions that you can change. The estimate assumes the shifted trips use walking, cycling or seats on buses that already run.

    • Shade. A tree line in the kerb zone cools the footpath and cycle track.
    • Flooding. Rain gardens soak up stormwater and pass the rest to a drain under the footpath.
    • Cleaner air at street level. Steady traffic burns less fuel than stop-and-go traffic.
    07 · ONE IDEA, FIVE THEMES

    How the proposal answers the challenge

    Primary theme

    Smart mobility and digital innovation

    Camera analytics, automatic plate reading, a public compliance dashboard and open lane data turn painted lines into a managed system.

    Mobility for all

    Every tier starts with a continuous footpath. Cyclists, including people who cannot afford a motor vehicle, get space of their own. Slow streets make colonies safe for children and older people.

    Future-ready public transport

    The widest roads give buses a priority lane, so the bus is faster than the car in peak hour. With the city about 3,385 buses short, every bus it has needs to move faster and carry more. Cycle tracks and footpaths bring people to bus stops and metro stations.

    Climate-smart Cyberabad

    Transport emits about 10,640 tonnes of CO2 a day. More trips by cycle and bus bring that down. The kerb zone is planted with trees for shade and built with rain gardens that soak up stormwater.

    Behaviour change

    A city-wide colour code, a warning-first period, corridor scores and fleet pledges make lane discipline a shared habit.

    08 · ROLLOUT

    Start with paint, build for 25 years

    1. 0 to 6 monthsMeasure every road of 18 m and wider and assign each a tier. Pilot four corridors using paint, bollards and lane cameras, starting with Khajaguda–Nanakramguda Road.
    2. 6 to 24 monthsPublish pilot results. Extend to the main IT corridor roads. Add mid-block cameras and the public dashboard. Connect new cycle tracks to the ORR cycle track.
    3. 2 to 5 yearsReplace paint with permanent kerbs, shade trees and rain gardens. Open bus priority lanes on roads of 40 m and over.
    4. 5 to 25 yearsWrite the width rule into layout approvals, so that every new road in growth areas such as Kokapet is built with its lanes from the first day.

    The first phase needs paint, bollards, signs and software, and no new land.

    WorkProposed lead
    Road survey, lane marking, kerbs, footpaths, trees and rain gardensCyberabad Municipal Corporation

    Camera enforcement of the existing lane rules, lay-bys and message boards on the ORRHyderabad Growth Corridor Limited, the ORR authority, with traffic police
    Lane champions, tech park and resident association outreach, fleet pledgesSociety for Cyberabad Security Council

    These are our suggestions for who should lead. None of these bodies has been consulted.

    Give every road user a lane. Give every lane a camera that understands it.
